chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Wider Lens on Risk

lessons.title: Beyond Volatility: Liquidity, Valuation, Leverage and Manager Risk

children.text: Four investors, four losses, and not one of them would have shown up as volatility. Rohit needed cash for a medical emergency and had to sell his Thane flat 15% below the going rate. Sana's startup shares were valued at three times her cost, until the next funding round priced them at half. Karthik's leveraged second home fell 10% in value and wiped out most of his down payment. Meera's fund manager left the firm, and the fund's strategy drifted into deals she had never signed up for. Chapter 1 showed that volatility misses a lot. This lesson names the four risks it misses most and gives you a way to score any asset on each.

body.text: Before you compare the return of any alternative with a traditional asset, ask four questions: Can I get out? Who says what it is worth? How much borrowed money is inside? How much depends on one manager? Volatility answers none of them.

stats.label: Liquidity risk
stats.context: At a fair price, when I need to

stats.label: Valuation risk
stats.context: Who sets it, how often, with what bias

children.text: 1. Liquidity Risk: Can You Get Out?

markDefs.definition: How quickly you can sell an asset without having to accept a noticeably lower price.
Contractual limits on when you can take money out, such as lock-in periods, fixed fund tenures or restrictions on transfers.

children.text: Liquidity risk comes in two forms.
Market liquidity
is about finding a buyer: a flat or an unlisted share can legally be sold any day, but the buyer might take six months to appear or demand a steep discount.
Structural liquidity
is about the rules: a close-ended AIF simply does not let you out before its tenure ends, however willing you are to take a loss.
Three things make liquidity risk more dangerous than it looks:
It disappears when you need it most.
During the 2020 lockdown, property registrations in Indian cities dropped to a small fraction of normal levels. Buyers vanished exactly when many sellers wanted cash.
It is priced as a discount, not a delay.
If you must sell quickly, the price you accept is the real cost, and it can wipe out years of income.
Your whole life is not illiquid.
Job losses, medical bills and family needs arrive on their own schedule. An asset that cannot meet them forces you to sell something else, often at a bad time.

body.title: Show me the cost of a forced sale

children.text: Rohit's Thane flat would fetch ₹80 lakh with a patient six-month search. He needs the money in five weeks, so he accepts a 15% discount.

cells: Fair value with a patient sale

children.text: One rushed sale erased six years of rent. A Nifty 50 ETF sold on the same day would have gone at the market price, whatever that price was.
2. Valuation Risk: Is the Value Real?

markDefs.definition: Estimating an asset's value with a financial model and assumptions, because there is no active market price to use.

children.text: A listed share's value is whatever the last trade on NSE says. An alternative's value is usually
marked to model

: someone chooses a method, picks comparable deals, and makes assumptions about rents, growth or exit prices. Valuation risk is the chance that this number is stale, optimistic, or simply wrong, and that you find out only when you try to sell.

body.caption: Who values what, and how often (typical practice)

cells: The market, through trades on NSE and BSE
Market price for units; a registered valuer for the underlying NAV
Price daily; NAV from periodic valuations
Units can trade well above or below NAV
An independent valuer, using the manager's inputs
The last funding round, or a dealer quote
Round prices often include special rights you do not have
A broker's estimate or recent sales nearby
The price you hope for, not the price someone pays

children.text: Byju's shows how far a private valuation can travel. The edtech company was valued at about $22 billion in a 2022 funding round. Over the next two years, as its finances and governance came under scrutiny, several of its own investors marked their stakes down sharply, some to near zero. Anyone who had treated the 2022 number as money in the bank had been measuring a price that no buyer would pay.

body.text: Watch for conflicts of interest. Fund managers often earn fees linked to the value of the assets they manage, and platforms benefit when their deals look successful. A valuation is only as trustworthy as the independence of whoever produced it.

children.text: 3. Leverage Risk: How Much Is Borrowed?

markDefs.definition: Loan-to-value: the loan amount as a percentage of the asset's value. An ₹80 lakh loan on a ₹1 crore flat is an 80% LTV.

children.text: Most Indians who own property as an investment use a home loan, often at a high
LTV

. Borrowed money magnifies every move in the asset's value, measured against the much smaller amount of your own money in it. Here is the rough formula for the return on your own money, or equity, in a single year:

body.caption: R_A = asset return (price change plus rent), L = loan share of value, r = loan interest rate, E = equity share of value

children.text: Karthik buys a ₹1 crore flat in Bengaluru with ₹20 lakh of his own money and an ₹80 lakh loan at 8%. Rent yields 2.5% a year. Compare one good year and one bad year against buying the same flat entirely with cash.

body.caption: One year, with and without a home loan (illustrative, before tax and other costs)

cells: Karthik: gain or loss in rupees

children.text: Notice the asymmetry. Because the loan costs 8% while the flat earns only 7.5% in a good year, leverage actually made Karthik's good year worse than the cash buyer's. In a bad year, it turned a 7.5% dip into a loss of almost 70% of his own money. And the EMIs keep coming either way.

body.title: Leverage in a falling market
body.prompt: An investor buys a commercial unit with 25% of their own money and a 75% loan. Ignore interest and rent. If the unit's value falls 20%, what percentage of the investor's own money is lost?
body.explanation: On a ₹1 crore unit, equity is ₹25 lakh. A 20% fall is ₹20 lakh, all of which comes out of the owner's equity because the loan must still be repaid in full. ₹20 lakh ÷ ₹25 lakh = 80%. With leverage, a 20% fall in the asset is an 80% fall for you.

body.text: Leverage can also sit inside the structure, where you do not see it. A REIT borrows at the trust level, which SEBI caps at 49% of the value of its assets. Category III AIFs can use leverage through derivatives. Category I and II AIFs cannot borrow except temporarily for operational needs. Always ask how much debt sits between you and the asset.

children.text: 4. Manager Risk: Who Is Driving?

In a Nifty 50 index fund, the manager barely matters. Every fund holds the same 50 stocks, and returns differ by fractions of a percent. In alternatives, picking the manager or the deal is most of the decision. The gap between the best and worst managers is so wide that the "average" return of an asset class tells you little about what you will actually get.

body.title: Illustrative gap between top-quartile and bottom-quartile managers (percentage points a year)

children.text: Manager risk is not only about skill. It shows up in four ways:
Skill.
Some managers consistently pick better deals, and most do not.
Key person risk.
The partner whose track record you bought into can leave, fall ill or retire in the middle of a seven-year fund.
Style drift.
A fund raised for senior secured loans slowly moves into riskier structured deals to keep its return target alive.
Governance and integrity.
Weak controls, related-party deals or diversion of money.

The Amrapali case is a painful Indian example of the last point, from the world of property. Tens of thousands of homebuyers in Noida and Greater Noida paid for flats that were never delivered. In 2019, the Supreme Court found that homebuyers' money had been diverted, cancelled the group's RERA registrations and directed the state-owned NBCC to complete the stalled projects. The buyers had judged the flats. The real risk was the people managing their money.

body.title: Which risk is it?
body.question: A private credit AIF was raised to make senior secured loans to profitable mid-sized companies. Three years in, to keep its 14% target return, it starts funding unsecured loans to early-stage real estate projects. Which risk has increased most directly?
options: Market liquidity risk of the fund's units
body.explanation: The manager has moved away from the strategy investors signed up for. That is style drift, a form of manager risk. It will likely raise default risk too, but the root cause is the manager's decision, not borrowing or market volatility.

body.title: Name the ratio
body.textWithBlank: A ₹60 lakh home loan on a ₹75 lakh flat means the loan-to-value ratio is ___ percent.
body.explanation: ₹60 lakh ÷ ₹75 lakh = 0.80, or an 80% LTV. The owner's equity is only 20% of the flat's value, so every 1% fall in the flat's price is a 5% fall in the owner's equity.

body.title: Score the pre-IPO pitch
body.scenario: Ishaan, a 36-year-old product manager in Noida, is offered ₹8 lakh worth of pre-IPO shares in a profitable logistics startup through an unlisted share dealer. The dealer says the shares are "valued at ₹640 based on the last funding round" and that an IPO is "expected in 12 to 18 months." The company has no debt. There is a six-month lock-in on pre-IPO shares after listing.
body.prompt: Score this investment Low, Medium or High on each of the four risks, and give a one-line reason for each.
body.modelAnswer:
Liquidity risk: High. There is no exchange before listing, the dealer's buy-back price may be far below ₹640, the IPO timeline is not guaranteed, and the post-listing lock-in adds at least six more months.

Valuation risk: High. ₹640 comes from a funding round in which investors likely had preference rights Ishaan will not get, and the dealer's markup is unknown. The IPO price could be set well below it.

Leverage risk: Low. The company has no debt and Ishaan is paying cash. (It would become high if he borrowed to buy.)

Manager risk: Medium to high. His outcome depends on the founders' execution and governance, and on the IPO actually happening, with far less disclosure than a listed company provides.

Overall: three of four risks score high, and none of them would show up as volatility, because there is no daily price to measure.

points: Volatility misses the four risks that matter most in alternatives: liquidity, valuation, leverage and manager risk.
Liquidity risk is both finding a buyer (market liquidity) and being allowed to leave (structural liquidity), and it vanishes in exactly the moments you need it.
Appraised and model-based values can be stale or optimistic. Byju's went from a $22 billion private valuation to heavy markdowns within about two years.
Leverage magnifies losses on your own money: with 25% equity, a 20% fall in the asset wipes out 80% of your stake.
In alternatives, the gap between good and bad managers is far wider than in index funds, and governance failures like Amrapali can outweigh the quality of the asset itself.
Score every alternative on all four risks before you compare its return with a traditional asset.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or avoid any property, fund, company or security. Examples and figures are illustrative unless stated otherwise. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
